items.title: Oxygen-Stoichiometry-Driven Crossover from Polaronic Insulator to Superconductor in Orthorhombic Ti9O10 Films
authors: Zongyao Huang, 宗耀 黄, Wei Hu, 卫 胡, Zhiwei Wang, 智炜 王, Shihao Liu, 仕豪 刘, Huiyu Wang, 慧宇 王, Yanjun Li, 彦君 李, Xiangyu Hua, 翔宇 华, Zhaohang Li, 朝航 李, Feixiong Quan, 飞熊 全, Zhengjie Wang, 郑杰 王, Ying Feng, 颖 冯, Zhen Wang, 臻 王, Jing Tao, 婧 陶, Xigang Luo, 习刚 罗, Jianjun Ying, 剑俊 应, Tao Wu, 涛 吴, Xianhui Chen and 仙辉 陈
items.summary: The Bardeen–Cooper–Schrieffer theory of superconductivity is restricted to weak electron–phonon coupling. In the strong-coupling regime, charge carriers self-trap via local lattice distortions, forming polarons whose condensation provides an alternative mechanism for superconductivity. Titanium oxides serve as a model system for polaron physics, suggesting the possibility of polaronic superconductivity. Here we report oxygen-stoichiometry-driven crossover from polaronic insulator to superconductor in epitaxial Ti9O10 thin films. Temperature-dependent Raman spectroscopy supports the films as a potential polaronic insulator, in which oxygen stoichiometry control reveals an anticorrelation between the polaronic insulating state and superconductivity. Tuning the oxygen pressure suppresses the polaronic insulating state and induces superconductivity, resulting in two distinct superconducting regions in the oxygen–pressure phase diagram. Our results provide a pathway toward understanding superconductivity in polaronic materials and offer a route for searching high-temperature superconductors.

items.title: Medium Electrical Conductivity Governs the Collective Behaviors of Quincke Rollers
authors: Zihan Qiao, 子涵 乔, Jingrui Gu, 京瑞 顾, Jiayu Liu, 佳钰 刘, Guomeng Wang, 国猛 王, Hao Lu, 灏 卢, Ting Kuang, 婷 况, Bo Zhang, 波 张, Wei Wang and 威 王
items.summary: Active matter systems can convert environmental energy into continuous motion and exhibit collective behaviors. As a typical electrically driven active particle system, Quincke rollers can display a variety of collective behaviors under a uniform DC electric field. However, a systematic understanding of the emergence and evolution of different collective behaviors is still lacking, and it remains unclear how external environmental conditions, such as temperature and humidity, influence the dynamics of collective behaviors. In this work, we find that increasing temperature and humidity drives a continuous transition of the collective behavior of Quincke rollers from vortices to polar clusters, rotating clusters, and finally active crystals. In situ electrical measurements show that the medium conductivity increases by nearly 10-fold as the temperature rises from 20 ℃ to 60 ℃, and by approximately 30-fold as the relative humidity increases from 5% to 65%, whereas the permittivity changes by about 10−15%. Finite-element calculations further reveal that the increase in medium electrical conductivity strongly modifies the magnitudes of the electric dipolar and hydrodynamic interactions between rollers. These forces shift from pure repulsion to anisotropic attraction and then to isotropic attraction, resulting in the emergence of vortices, polar clusters, rotating clusters, and active crystals in turn. These results provide a simple physical picture linking the conductivity of the medium to the collective states in Quincke roller system and establish a theoretical framework that incorporates dipolar interaction, hydrodynamic interaction, and electro-hydrodynamic interaction for understanding the dynamics of collective behavior. In addition, this work demonstrates that temperature and humidity can serve as simple, efficient, and reversible control parameters for the in situ regulation of the collective behaviors of Quincke rollers.

items.title: Power-Law Quasiperiodic Criticality in a Non-Hermitian Ising Chain
authors: Wen-Long You and 文龙 尤
items.summary: We study a non-Hermitian Ising chain with a power-law quasiperiodic field hj = hcosp(2παj+ϕ), where the positive integer p controls the power of the modulation. The model admits an exact site-factorized similarity transformation that maps the quasi-Hermitian regime onto a real quasiperiodic Ising chain. We derive the exact zero-mode edge-localization boundary and show that the critical field on the quasi-Hermitian branch scales as 2p, while the associated localization-length exponent remains unity for all p. At the boundary, the variance of the logarithmic coupling fluctuations is enhanced exactly by a factor of p2. In the quasi-Hermitian regime, the factorized similarity transformation shows that the spatial biorthogonal entanglement spectrum is identical to that of the Hermitian counterpart. The half-chain entanglement entropy exhibits approximately logarithmic growth over the accessible sizes, with a p-dependent finite-size slope. We finally discuss a possible realization using state-selective loss and conditional no-jump dynamics.

items.title: Giant Planar Hall Effect of Unprecedented Amplitude in n-HgTe with Extremely Low Electron Density
authors: A.T. Lonchakov, S.B. Bobin and S.D. Popov
items.summary: We report the observation of a giant planar Hall effect in an n-HgTe single crystal with an extremely low electron density of 7.3×1014 cm−3. Its amplitude reaches an unprecedented value of 0.9 Ohm·cm at T = 40 K and in a magnetic field of 10 T—to the best of our knowledge, the highest ever reported for this effect in any topological material. We attribute the strong magnetoresistance anisotropy underlying the giant planar Hall effect to the coexistence of a topological Weyl semimetal phase and a trivial gapless phase in the band spectrum of a bulk n-HgTe. The former gives rise to strong negative longitudinal magnetoresistance driven by chiral anomaly, whereas the latter leads to charge compensation-induced positive transverse magnetoresistance without saturation. We have established that it is precisely this magnetoresistance that provides the dominant contribution to the giant amplitude of the planar Hall effect. The observed giant planar Hall effect in this particular n-HgTe sample suggests that low-density mercury telluride merits further investigation as a candidate material for exploring chiral-anomaly transport and for potential sensor applications.

items.title: Electron–Phonon Coupling Drives the Gapless Charge Density Wave in Few-Layer 1T-VSe2
authors: Yonglong Cheng, 咏龙 程, Yimanqi He, 逸蔓奇 何, Xiangfan Xu and 象繁 徐
items.summary: The driving mechanism of the charge density wave (CDW) remains debated, particularly between Fermi surface nesting (FSN) and electron–phonon coupling (EPC) scenarios. Here, gate-tunable electrical and thermoelectric transport measurements were used to probe the CDW-related electronic structure in few-layer 1T-VSe2. Thickness reduction strongly suppresses the long-range three-dimensional CDW order associated with the bulk transition near 110 K, allowing the high-temperature CDW-related anomaly near 170 K to be resolved in macroscopic transport. Through gate tuning, we find that this CDW-related state does not exhibit signatures of a well-defined Peierls-like gap but instead remains gapless within an intrinsic multiband electronic landscape. In particular, the Seebeck coefficient shows pronounced anomalies at both temperature scales (110 K and 170 K), yet no gap-induced thermoelectric anomaly or gate-dependent gap-opening behavior is observed. These results demonstrate the gapless nature of the CDW state, while the high-temperature 170 K anomaly directly fingerprints the localized precursor lattice softening, collectively providing strong transport evidence that supports EPC over conventional FSN as the dominant driving mechanism. Our work provides a new experimental perspective on the dimensionality-dependent CDW behavior in VSe2 and establishes thermoelectric transport as a sensitive probe for distinguishing CDW formation mechanisms in low-dimensional materials.

items.title: Quantum predator-prey cycles in dissipative Rydberg array
items.summary: Abstract The predator-prey cycle is a paradigmatic example of self-organized population oscillations in far-from-equilibrium systems, yet testing its underlying mechanism in natural ecosystems is often precluded by uncontrollable microscopic parameters. Here, we propose a quantum analogue of predator-prey dynamics using a tunable two-dimensional Rydberg atom array. Through mean-field analysis and large-scale numerical simulations based on the open-system discrete truncated Wigner approximation, we demonstrate stable predator-prey cycles of Rydberg excitations on microsecond timescales. We show that nonperturbative quantum coherence drives spontaneous time-translation symmetry breaking, leading to globally synchronized oscillations under short-range interactions. Even under desynchronization caused by quantum jumps, locally synchronized predator-prey cycles persist, with amplitude scaling inversely with the square root of the system size. Our work extends the study of predator-prey models to the quantum realm and advances quantum simulation strategies that leverage engineered many-body nonequilibrium effects.

items.title: Self-evolving Embodied AI
items.summary: Abstract Embodied Artificial Intelligence (AI) is an intelligent system formed by agents and their environment through active perception, embodied cognition, and action interaction. Existing embodied AI remains confined to human-crafted setting, in which agents are trained on given memories and construct models for given tasks, enabling fixed physical embodiments to interact with relatively static environments. Such methods fail in in-the-wild setting characterized by variable physical embodiments and dynamic open environments. This paper introduces self-evolving embodied AI, a new paradigm in which agents operate based on their changing physical embodiment and environment through five software-level components, namely memory self-updating, task self-switching, environment self-prediction, embodiment self-adaptation, and model self-evolution, together with a hardware-level component for physical embodiment evolution, aiming to achieve continually adaptive intelligence through software-hardware co-evolution. Specifically, we present the definition, framework, components, mechanisms, roadmap, and evaluation indicators of self-evolving embodied AI, systematically review state-of-the-art works for realized components, discuss practical applications, and point out future research directions. We believe that self-evolving embodied AI enables agents to autonomously learn and interact with environments in a human-like manner and provides a new perspective toward general artificial intelligence.

items.title: Stable and selective C(sp3)–H halogenation over COF-modified β-Fe2O3 photoanodes
items.summary: Abstract Photoelectrocatalytic synthesis provides a sustainable route to high-value organic chemicals, yet achieving high selectivity while maintaining long-term stability remains challenging because of limited interfacial reactant availability and competing radical-mediated reaction pathways. Here, we develop a COF-modified photoanode by integrating a functionalized covalent organic framework (COF) onto β -Fe 2 O 3 to regulate aqueous C( sp 3 )–H halogenation. Using cyclohexane chlorination as a model reaction, the COF-modified β -Fe 2 O 3 photoanode achieves a monochlorination selectivity of up to 96.8% under AM 1.5 G illumination (100 mW cm −2 ), far exceeding the 53.9% obtained over bare β -Fe 2 O 3 . Under one-sun illumination, the photoanode delivers a photocurrent density of 2.8 mA cm −2 and remains stable for 300 h, retaining approximately 95% chlorocyclohexane selectivity at the end of the test. Even under 13-sun illumination, the photocurrent density reaches approximately 35 mA cm −2 , with a chlorocyclohexane selectivity of 91.9% after 100 h. The COF-modified photoanode also shows enhanced monobromination and monoiodination selectivities, demonstrating the generality of this approach.

items.title: Temperature-dependent Raman signatures of local symmetry breaking in vacancy-ordered double perovskite Cs2SnI6
authors: Tomke E. Glier, Nicholas J. Weadock, Julian A. Vigil, Cole Shank, Xixi Qin, Gabriel J. Graf, Hemamala I. Karunadasa, Volker Blum, Michael F. Toney, Dmitry Reznik
items.summary: Despite their apparent symmetry, halide perovskites can host hidden distortions that affect their properties. Using temperature-dependent Raman spectroscopy and first-principles calculations, Glier et al. observed that symmetry-forbidden phonons emerged in the vacancy-ordered double perovskite Cs2SnI6 at low temperatures, despite the persistence of the average cubic structure. A common activation energy of 15–20 meV characterizes the temperature-dependent Raman response, while enhanced multi-phonon scattering highlights strong electron-phonon coupling, demonstrating Raman spectroscopy as a sensitive probe of hidden local structural behavior.

items.title: Confinement-induced bound state and effective potential for microwave-shielded ultracold molecules
items.summary: We investigate the bound state and effective potential of microwave-shielded ultracold molecules under longitudinal confinement, which effectively creates a quasi-two-dimensional (q2D) geometry. We find that the longitudinal confinement facilitates bound-state formation in both bosonic and fermionic molecules, leading to confinement-induced bound states that are absent in free space. To describe these bound states, we establish an effective 2D potential by incorporating the full interaction effect along the longitudinal direction. Compared with other simplified 2D potentials, the effective potential accurately predicts the binding energies of ultracold molecules over a much broader parameter regime of microwave coupling and confinement strength. Remarkably, it can even predict deep bound states with binding energies well exceeding the confinement frequency. By establishing this effective potential, our work paves the way for efficiently exploring the rich low-dimensional physics of microwave-shielded ultracold molecules.

items.title: Bearing, heading and the perceptual geometry of collective motion
items.summary: Traditional models of collective motion commonly assume that animals turn to match their neighbours' directions of travel. In the harmonic theory, decisions follow from a neural representation of direction, and a neighbour enters only as a stimulus at a bearing, the direction in which it lies. Here we show that a neighbour's spatial extent allows its orientation to enter through projection geometry alone, and the theory generates a matrix of coupling coefficients indexed by the neighbour's bearing and aspect. Responses to bearing alone form one edge of this matrix, and classical heading matching is a special case on its diagonal, one ray through a two-parameter family. Independently, an animal that responds only to neighbour position, perceived with a delay, acquires an alignment coefficient set by the slope of its distance-weighted attraction profile, so that it can align, anti-align or reverse sign. Alignment need not be a rule to be measured. In schooling fish and walking pigeons with body orientation measured independently of travel, social responses are recovered, including bearing responses in the fish. Heading excess depends on how turning is measured, appearing in the fish with forward but not centred responses and remaining unresolved in pigeons. Controls show why neither outcome identifies a direct alignment rule. In fish recordings with motion-assigned body polarity, heading-dependent structure departs from Vicsek form and fails the coefficient test for a common angular potential. Whether animals align thereby becomes a measurable question, with geometric, perceptual and behavioural origins that can be distinguished.

items.title: Fractional Quantum Hall States: Infinite Matrix Product Representation and its Implications
items.summary: We present a novel matrix product representation of the Laughlin and related fractional quantum Hall wavefunctions based on a rigorous version of the correlators of a chiral quantum field theory. This representation enables the quantitative control of the coefficients of the Laughlin wavefunction times an arbitrary monomial symmetric polynomial when expanded in a Slater determinant or permanent basis. It renders the properties, such as factorization and the renewal structure, inherent in such fractional quantum Hall wavefunctions transparent. We prove bounds on the correlators of the chiral quantum field theory and utilize this representation to demonstrate the exponential decay of connected correlations and a gap in the entanglement spectrum on a thin cylinder.

items.title: A High-Dimensional Lab-Frame Model of Markovian Dynamics in Alanine Dipeptide
items.summary: We present a high-dimensional coarse-grained model of alanine dipeptide that explicitly incorporates global translation and rotation alongside internal conformational dynamics. Using atomistic molecular dynamics trajectories, we construct a 10-bead Markovian Langevin model with a 24-dimensional internal potential of mean force and a full matrix of site-specific friction coefficients. The equilibrium landscape is represented by a Gaussian mixture model, while a rotational-entropy correction accounts for the coupling between internal conformation and global molecular motion. Friction coefficients are obtained using a generalized Einstein relation based on time-correlation functions. We show that the rotational-entropy correction is essential for obtaining a physically admissible friction matrix and significantly affects the inferred dynamics. Without fitting to coarse-grained dynamical observables, the resulting model reproduces a broad range of atomistic auto- and cross-correlation functions. The result is a compact and interpretable dynamical representation of the entire peptide at the chosen CG resolution, which explicitly preserves distinctions between energetic and dissipative coupling over a wide range of motions, including those between conformational fluctuations and global translational and rotational diffusion.

items.title: Barlow Packings All Have Maximum Packing Fraction: Why it is so Hard to Find Barlow Structures Other than fcc or hcp?
items.summary: We apply lattice theory to periodic Barlow packings $(X_{1}X_{2}\dots X_{N})_{\infty}$ where $X_{i}\in\{A,B,C\}$ and $X_{i}\neq X_{i+1}$, formed by stacking two-dimensional hexagonal close-packed layers, interacting via generalized $(n,m)$-Lennard-Jones potentials. The cohesive energies of all packings lie between those of hexagonal close-packed (hcp, $(AB)$) and face-centered cubic (fcc, $(ABC)$) structure and vary almost linearly with the fcc stacking fraction. The equilibrium lattice constant, bulk modulus, Einstein frequency, and vibrational entropy show similarly near-linear trends. For the standard $(12,6)$ potential, fcc has the highest vibrational entropy and hcp the lowest, with other Barlow packings falling between them, consistent with previous sticky-hard-sphere Monte Carlo simulations and supported by phonon dispersion calculations. These trends imply an approximately linear dependence of free energy on fcc stacking fraction, with hcp and fcc as endpoints. This provides a simple thermodynamic explanation for why intermediate Barlow stackings are rare in nature: near-linearity offers little driving force to favor them. Exceptions may arise when hcp and fcc are nearly degenerate in energy or when many-body interactions, absent from the present model, favor another stacking. Density-functional calculations including dispersion forces for argon Barlow packings with periods $N=2,3,4$, and $12$ corroborate the predicted near-linear cohesive energy dependence.

items.title: On the critical value of void percolation in high dimensions
items.summary: In the random Lorentz gas, a point tracer moves through spherical obstacles of (reduced) density $Φ$ centered on a Poisson point process in $d$-dimensional space, $\mathbb{R}^d$, and becomes localized once the vacant space stops percolating, at $Φ_{\rm p}(d)$. The dimensional scaling of this void percolation threshold has remained elusive. Prior bounds, conjectural ones included, ranged from $Ω(1)$ to $O(d\ln d)$, leaving even the scaling undetermined. We here prove that $Φ_{\rm p}(d)=Θ(d)$, and in particular that $\tfrac12\,d \le Φ_{\rm p}(d) \le 5\,d$ for all sufficiently large $d$. The upper bound counts hierarchical families of escape waypoints called tree embeddings; the lower bound is via a weighted second-moment estimate on an explicit ensemble of ballistic escape routes. A linear scaling of $Φ_{\rm p}(d)$ excludes the $d\ln d$ growth suggested by analogy with other systems in the random first-order transition universality class and is consistent with the numerical estimate $Φ_{\rm p}/d \to 3.40(5)$. Because the mean-field dynamical transition is likewise linear, $Φ_{\rm d}\simeq 2.40\,d$, our result fixes the activated window $[Φ_{\rm d},Φ_{\rm p}]$ as a bounded---rather than diverging---correction to mean-field dynamical arrest in sufficiently high $d$.

items.title: Thermally-driven quantum reservoir computing
items.summary: Heat generation limits computation, classical and quantum, from single logic gates to entire data centers. However, an in principle limiting physical factor can sometimes be turned into a resource. In reservoir computing, energy dissipation is what gives a reservoir its fading memory. Here, we introduce a paradigm where the data injection itself is encoded on the time-dependent temperature of a thermal bath. We derive an exact expression for the nonlinear response of any fixed readout, and prove a rigorous memory-nonlinearity trade-off which turns out to be a structural necessity, rather than a tunable dynamical regime, since the same coupling that injects data also enforces equilibration. We illustrate both results with a driven qubit, using a single free parameter, and with a pair of coupled qubits, where the breaking of a discrete symmetry opens a fifteen-dimensional space to a single observable, yet that observable alone recovers just over half of it. This refutes the misconception that large Hilbert spaces guarantee computational power. Our results relocate the memory-nonlinearity trade-off from the reservoir's dynamics to its measurement channel, pointing to observable choice and bath engineering (instead of Hamiltonian control) as the physical levers for a thermally-native quantum reservoir computer.

items.title: Nonperturbative optomechanics with thin, weakly reflective intracavity dielectrics
items.summary: Levitated dielectric sensors are often treated as perturbative probes of a pre-existing optical field. We show that this picture fails for a novel sensor geometry: a dielectric plate whose transverse extent captures the full optical mode. Even an optically thin sensor with modest refractive index can heavily restructure the intracavity fields, effectively partitioning a cavity into two subcavities with substantial cross-coupling and producing new optical resonances and trapping sites with properties which deviate from the standard intuition. Conventional perturbative expressions for the cavity frequency shift and optomechanical coupling depart from the exact solution at thicknesses as small as $\simλ/(10n)$. Furthermore, cavity locking decreases the coupling and increases the trap stiffness by orders of magnitude, and the coupled subcavity structure permits appreciable optical cooling at zero detuning, a distinct behavior unique to this nonperturbative regime. These effects, sharing a common origin, establish a distinct regime of cavity optomechanics in which the sensor is no longer merely a probe of the cavity field, but an element that helps define it.

items.title: Statistical properties of quantum jumps between macroscopic states of light: reading an operational coherence record
items.summary: We propose an experimental apparatus to reveal the quantum coherence manifested in downward quantum jumps of amplitude bistability. The underlying coherent superposition of macroscopic quantum states is translated into the statistical properties of the integrated charge deposited in the detector circuit of a mode-matched heterodyne/homodyne detection scheme. At first, the dynamical evolution of a signal transmitted from an auxiliary cavity is employed to pinpoint a macroscopic switching event in a bistable main cavity subject to direct photodetection. Once the decision is made on the occurrence of a downward switch, the main cavity mode is let to freely decay to the vacuum, monitored to the production of an integrated charge. In the long-time limit, the charge distribution over an identical collection of pure states generated during the jumps converges to the Q function (heterodyne detection) or marginals of the Wigner function (homodyne detection) dictated by the phase of the local oscillator. When fluctuations over the ensemble step in, we connect the statistical properties of several switching events and the ensuing production of current records, to the cavity field correlations associated with the breakdown of photon blockade.

items.title: The lattice Boltzmann machine
items.summary: The lattice Boltzmann (LB) method is widely regarded as a very flexible and efficient solver for a broad class of transport phenomena in fluids, soft matter and related fields. In this paper, we posit that such flexibility is a direct result of its generative nature as a rule-driven information-processing machine. Its update, a relaxation toward a local target followed by a shift along the lattice, belongs to the same class of iterated relaxation dynamics as residual networks and transformers, with the difference that in LB the operators are fixed by conservation and symmetry rather than learned from data. We show that three properties of this update are sufficient to promote the emergence of closed macroscopic laws from the underlying iteration process, the physical content of the target deciding the specific law in question. A machine whose target is drawn at random generates the transport law predicted from its moments. A network given the same three properties on a graph, where there is no lattice, is trained on a traffic process and generates a conservation law of its own. The mechanism has a precise limit, where the damping of the non-conserved modes fails, and on the lattice the macroscopic law gives no warning of it. In this reading, LB is a lattice Boltzmann machine whose informing rules are supplied by physics rather than by training. Its three properties then state what a new ingredient should preserve when it enters an LB model, whether it comes from physics or from data.

items.title: Exact magnetic ground states and competing interlayer exchanges in layered kagome magnets
items.summary: Magnetic ground states in layered kagome magnets are investigated using a Heisenberg model with six interlayer exchange interactions. For isotropic two-sublattice models with identical diagonal Fourier exchange functions, a coplanar single-wave-vector ground state is shown to exist for arbitrary exchange ranges. Extending the three-exchange model of Rosenfeld and Mushnikov reveals that longer-range interactions can change the preferred magnetic order from spiral to ferromagnetic and back to spiral, rather than merely modifying the spiral period. The analysis includes ground-state phase diagrams, harmonic stability, magnetic-field response, and sensitivity to individual exchange interactions. The propagation vector, internal layer angle, saturation field, and planar susceptibility are also found to be insufficient to determine all six exchange constants uniquely. These results provide a basis for predicting noncollinear magnetic order from first-principles exchange interactions.

items.title: Gate-tunable Josephson parametric amplifiers based on semiconductor nanowires
items.summary: Superconductor-semiconductor hybrid materials have been extensively used for experiments on electrically tunable quantum devices. Notably, Josephson junctions utilizing nanowire weak links have enabled a number of new gate-tunable qubits, including gatemons, Andreev level qubits and spin qubits. Conversely, superconducting parametric amplifiers based on Josephson junctions have not yet been implemented using nanowires, even though such nearly quantum limited amplifiers are key elements in experiments on quantum circuits. Here we present Josephson parametric amplifiers based on arrays of parallel InAs nanowires that feature a large critical current as required for linear amplification. The resonance frequency of the devices is gate-tunable by almost 1 GHz, with a gain exceeding 20 dB in multiple frequencies and markedly improved noise performance compared to a low-temperature commercial amplifier. This platform enables on-chip integration of gate-tunable qubits with nearly quantum limited amplifiers using the same hybrid materials and on any substrate.

items.title: Data-Driven Modeling of Molten Chloride Corrosion Using Static Test Data
items.summary: Molten chloride corrosion has been studied for decades, yet reliable prediction across different alloys, salts, and test conditions remains difficult. In this work, 291 static molten chloride corrosion experiments reported in the literature were compiled into a structured dataset and used to develop an interpretable machine-learning framework for corrosion-rate predictions. To better represent the differences in salt condition across studies, a Chloride Salt Preparation Index (CSPI) was introduced to bring the reported salt-treatment method, atmosphere control, and pre-exposure impurity condition on a common numerical scale. A blended tree-based ensemble provided the most consistent predictive performance, achieving a cross-validated \(R^2\) of 0.85 and an MAE of 0.41 mg cm\(^{-2}\) day\(^{-1}\). The graded CSPI retained more useful information than a simple purified/unpurified classification and emerged as the dominant model descriptor. Global sensitivity and SHAP analyses further identified exposure time, temperature, and alloy chemistry as important contributors to the model predictions, with several observed trends consistent with the established molten-chloride corrosion behavior. The conformal prediction intervals were well calibrated, providing an estimate of prediction uncertainty in addition to the point prediction. Overall, the framework demonstrates that historical corrosion data can support quantitative, interpretable, and uncertainty-aware prediction when experimental context is represented explicitly, while also highlighting where more consistent reporting and targeted experiments are needed to improve future molten-salt corrosion models.

items.title: Principles of Quantum Communication Theory: A Modern Approach
items.summary: This is a preliminary version of a book in progress on the theory of quantum communication. We adopt an information-theoretic perspective throughout and give a comprehensive account of fundamental results in quantum communication theory from the past decade (and earlier), with an emphasis on the modern one-shot-to-asymptotic approach that underlies much of today's state-of-the-art research in this field. In Part I, we cover mathematical preliminaries and provide a detailed study of quantum mechanics from an information-theoretic perspective. We also provide an extensive and thorough review of quantum entropies, and we devote an entire chapter to the study of entanglement measures. Equipped with these essential tools, in Part II we study classical communication (with and without entanglement assistance), entanglement distillation, quantum communication, secret key distillation, and private communication. In Part III, we cover the latest developments in feedback-assisted communication tasks, such as quantum and classical feedback-assisted communication, LOCC-assisted quantum communication, and secret key agreement.

items.title: Flexoelectric Switching of Lock-and-Key Topological Bits
items.summary: Topological defects in nematic liquid crystals are high-energy sites of reduced order. We show that a point defect can be stabilized in pillbox-shaped pores. The pore shape promotes lock-and-key docking similar to that observed for colloidal particles. The defect docks in one lobe or the other, displaying bistability. Furthermore, the defect moves like a charged object in an external electric field. An in-plane field drives the defect from one lobe to the opposite lobe, where it remains once the field is removed. The velocity is linear in field strength and reverses with polarity, consistent with flexoelectric coupling. Within the pore, the nematic around the defect carries a positive bulk bound charge density, compensated by negative space charge in the rest of the fluid and on the bounding surfaces. The external field breaks the mirror symmetry of the pore and drives the defect motion. Defect displacement increases the component of the net dipole in the domain along the field. Antagonistic curvature in peanut-shaped pores repels the defect, allowing pore geometry to set distinct switching thresholds. The defects, while not topologically required, are long lived, so information can be stored in their position, allowing them to serve as topological bits. Arrays of topological bits store and rewrite binary information in defect positions, offering a route to reconfigurable, field-addressable soft materials.

items.title: Universal Negative Correlation between Nonreciprocity and Superconducting Transition Width in FeTe-Based Heterostructures
items.summary: Nonreciprocal charge transport in noncentrosymmetric superconductors probes broken symmetries and superconducting fluctuations and underpins the superconducting diode effect. Despite extensive studies, the factors governing its magnitude remain unclear. In this work, we use molecular beam epitaxy (MBE) to synthesize a broad family of FeTe-based superconducting heterostructures with top layers spanning topologically trivial versus nontrivial, layered versus nonlayered, and magnetic versus nonmagnetic materials. Through systematic first- and second-harmonic transport measurements, we find that the magnetochiral anisotropy coefficient $γ$ is insensitive to the top-layer crystal structure, lattice constant, thickness, topology, and magnetism, but exhibits a negative correlation with the superconducting transition width $ΔT$. Control measurements on superconducting stoichiometric FeTe films reveal much weaker nonreciprocity, confirming the essential role of interfacial inversion-symmetry breaking. Combined with a disorder-based theoretical model, our results establish a universal relationship: for comparable inversion-symmetry breaking, reduced interfacial disorder sharpens the superconducting transition and strongly enhances nonreciprocal transport in the Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless (BKT) transition regime. These findings identify $ΔT$ as a unifying parameter governing nonreciprocity across FeTe-based heterostructures, reconcile previously disparate observations, and establish a general framework for engineering enhanced nonreciprocal superconducting responses and exploring superconducting diode effects in nonlinear quantum devices.

items.title: Nonequilibrium Spin-Glass Order in a Long-Range Quantum Ising Glass and Its Sensitivity to Noise
items.summary: We study spin-glass order after a transverse-field quench in a long-range quantum Ising glass. The diagonal-ensemble Edwards-Anderson order coincides at the no-quench and zero-field endpoints, yet in between cold shells overshoot it and hot shells undershoot it. This stems from a competition in correlation space between the rigidity of populated eigenstates and the spread of their pair patterns. Under weak longitudinal dephasing the zero-field endpoint is exactly pinned while the characteristic finite-quench response fades, giving a self-referenced noise probe for quantum spin simulators.

items.title: Embodied physical learning: a trained bacterial cell wall can guide organism behavior
items.summary: Physical learning studies how physical systems themselves can be trained to perform learning tasks using physical laws. For instance, disordered spring networks can be trained by local rules to route a mechanical signal from one site in the network to another. Disordered spring networks play key roles in many facets of cell biology, not just in terms of mechanics, but also in terms of motility. How then can training on the substrate itself impact the action of an organism, such as a bacterium? Here, we train a spring-network model of the bacterial cell wall and embed it in a motile agent. The stimulus is the load the cell generates by colliding with a surface. The trained wall routes that load across the body to distant flagellar motors, where it drives stator release, and the resulting turn biases the cell toward escape and delays subsequent surface contacts. On the first near-wall tumble after entrapment, the trained cell recovers 89% of the advantage an ideal side-resolved controller provides. We call this arrangement embodied physical learning: the stimulus, the actuator, and the consequences all belong to the agent, and the training force scale is inherited from the agent's own sensing rather than imposed. An actuator with its own kinetics imposes a second, tighter constraint: the routed signal must switch the actuator within the stimulus window. We also find that behavior converges within a few hundred wall encounters, comparable to what a cell in sustained contact with structure experiences in a single generation, and that the routing survives continuous crosslink remodeling provided crucial, tension-bearing bonds are protected. Experimental tests of embodied physical learning are discussed.

items.title: Hereditary Effective Atom Theory for Large-Scale Atomic Structure Prediction
items.summary: Predicting the atomic structure of large systems requires simultaneous exploration of atomic positions, species, and, generally, the number of atoms. The combinatorial growth of possible arrangements can make this search difficult even for standard global optimization methods. We introduce Hereditary Effective Atom Theory (HEAT), which integrates Effective Atom Theory (EAT) into a genetic algorithm. HEAT combines EAT's continuous relaxation of atomic positions, species, and population with the global search capabilities of genetic algorithms. Central to the method is a crossover scheme that directly superimposes two parent structures and relaxes the combined structure. HEAT outperforms conventional genetic-algorithm baselines in recovering a missing 240-atom H sublattice, predicting a 364-atom edge-dislocation core, and reconstructing a 1150-atom interior region of twisted-bilayer $\mathrm{WSe_2}$ from experimental ptychographic constraints. These results demonstrate how continuous effective-atom relaxation improves the exploration of large combinatorial structure spaces.

items.title: Sudden disappearance of a bright exciton in solid helium
items.summary: Excitons, bound electron-hole pairs, are investigated extensively in optical spectra, where their wave vector is considered to be vanishing. Excitonic spectra as a function of wave vector are much less explored, both theoretically and with measurements of the loss function. Here, we uncover a striking angular dependence of excitonic spectra for the prototypical case of solid helium, where a prominent excitonic peak is completely suppressed for a momentum transfer in certain directions. The effect is entirely due to the electron-hole exchange interaction. This phenomenon leads to a counter-intuitive effect close to Bragg points, where an infinitesimal change of direction of wave vector is sufficient to change the spectrum dramatically. We explain in which way the nature of excitons makes such a scenario possible. We discuss the pressure dependence, point to experimental evidence for our findings, and predict under which circumstances dramatic angular dependencies may also be found in other materials.

items.title: PFAS-induced modulation of vesicle diffusiophoresis
items.summary: Understanding how per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) partition into biological membranes and alter their properties is central for elucidating PFAS toxicity. Here, we experimentally investigate how the partitioning of anionic PFAS affects the surface charge of phospholipid vesicles and consequently, their electrokinetically driven vesicle motion, in particular diffusiophoresis. We find that PFAS partitioning enhances vesicle diffusiophoresis, consistent with a model combining the Nernst-Planck and Langmuir adsorption equations. Desorption experiments, together with quartz crystal microbalance with dissipation monitoring (QCM-D), further reveal that substantial lipid loss occurs during PFAS partitioning. We attribute this loss to lipophobic interactions between the fluorocarbon chains of PFAS and the alkyl chains of lipids. Our findings provide new mechanistic insights into how PFAS may disrupt biological systems.

items.title: Specific absorption rate of uniaxial single-domain nanomagnets: stochastic spin dynamics versus linear response theory
items.summary: We compute the specific absorption rate of a uniaxial single-domain nanomagnet driven by an alternating magnetic field by two methods: i) direct numerical integration of the stochastic (Langevin) Landau--Lifshitz--Gilbert equation (the LLL approach), and ii) linear response theory (LRT) based on the Debye susceptibility with the Néel relaxation time $\ta$. We first analytically show that both methods are equivalent for small magnetic field amplitude, and then compute their deviation $Λ\equiv\SAR_{\LLL}/\SAR_{\LRT}-1$ as a function of the magnetic field amplitude for two temperatures chosen on opposite sides of the Debye resonance. One of the main results is that the sign and magnitude of $Λ$ are governed by the dimensionless product $\om\ta$, in addition to the linearity parameter $ξ=μ_{s}B_{0}/k_{B}T$ for the easy-axis geometry considered here. Indeed, below resonance ($\om\ta<1$), linear response theory overestimates the specific absorption rate, whereas above resonance ($\om\ta>1$, the regime typical of blocked nanoparticles) linear response theory can underestimate the specific absorption rate by up to $\sim70\%$ at $ξ\sim2$. We expect this work to provide a quantitative guidance for the use of linear response theory in magnetic hyperthermia and related nanoscale heat-transport problems, and to serve as a single-particle benchmark for extensions to many-spin and interacting systems.

items.title: Langmuir kinetics and totally asymmetric volume exclusion in linear chains via Fock space formalism
items.summary: Driven-diffusive systems combining spatial exclusion and bulk exchange, such as the totally asymmetric simple exclusion process coupled with Langmuir kinetics (TASEP-LK), serve as foundational models for particle transport in vehicular traffic, conveyor networks, and mesoscopic flow channels. In this work, we employ an exact Doi-Peliti field-theoretic operator formulation in Fock space to evaluate steady-state observables, continuous phase landscapes, and spatial correlations in finite linear chains up to $k = 16$. By introducing a decomposition in terms of biorthonormal eigenvectors for asymmetric non-Hermitian matrices, the stationary state is calculated directly from the kernel of the quasi-Hamiltonian, completely bypassing the computationally prohibitive complexity of full matrix diagonalization and time-dependent matrix exponentiation. Across distinct rate regimes and global parametric scans, our exact discrete calculations demonstrate that finite-size stochastic fluctuations naturally smear out singular domain walls, producing smooth density profiles and continuous phase crossovers. Finite-size scaling illustrates how local profiles systematically steepen toward the sharp domain wall predicted by continuum field theory as $k \to \infty$. Furthermore, two-point correlation analysis reveals that in slow-kinetics regimes, spatial fluctuations generate strong inter-site cumulants, causing standard mean-field approximations to systematically underestimate joint occupancy probabilities by 50\%. These findings emphasize the necessity of analytical methods for modeling mesoscopic transport systems and short traffic corridors where local stochastic fluctuations and spatial correlations dominate the stationary dynamics.

items.title: The 2d Ising Model on Hyperbolic Lattices and the Role of Boundary Conditions
items.summary: We investigate the role of boundary conditions in the critical behaviour of the ferromagnetic Ising model on regular hyperbolic tessellations. Using worm and Metropolis simulations, we compare open boundaries with wired boundaries implemented through a common auxiliary spin. For open boundaries, the susceptibility exhibits volume-based finite-size scaling with non-mean-field scaling exponents that are approximately stable across four tessellations, supporting the possibility of a common universality class. Comparisons with Binder crossings and susceptibility peaks reveal substantial finite-size effects. For wired boundaries, the central-to-auxiliary spin correlator exhibits radial scaling consistent with a mean-field magnetization exponent. The central-spin response to a uniform magnetic field provides a further consistency test of $δ=3$. Layer-resolved responses to a weak boundary field also reveal an enhancement of the induced magnetization towards the interior. Our results highlight the importance of boundary conditions and the distinction between interior and whole-system observables in characterizing critical phenomena on non-amenable lattices.

items.title: High-pressure elastic properties of GeO2 polymorphs up to 120 GPa
items.summary: We systematically investigated the phase stability, pressure dependence of the elastic properties, and elastic anisotropy of four GeO2 polymorphs: rutile-, CaCl2-, alpha-PbO2-, and pyrite-type phases using theoretical calculations based on density functional theory. The elastic constants were calculated at regular pressure intervals within the stability fields of each phase, as determined by static enthalpy calculations. We further employed a strain-coupled Landau free-energy expansion to describe the pressure evolution of the elastic response associated with the rutile- to CaCl2-type transition and elucidate the origin of the elastic softening near the transition. The rutile- to CaCl2-type phase transition is consistent with a Landau-type second-order transition. As the transition is approached, elastic softening develops in the rutile-type phase, resulting in anomalous pressure dependence of the bulk and shear moduli. The calculated elastic-wave anisotropy increases markedly near the transition, primarily due to the rapid reduction in shear-wave velocity, reaching a maximum of approximately 190% at 20 GPa. Following the transition, the anisotropy decreases sharply in the CaCl2-type phase and exhibits discontinuity at the CaCl2-type/alpha-PbO2-type phase boundary. The higher-pressure alpha-PbO2- and pyrite-type phases exhibit comparatively weak pressure dependence of anisotropy, with small discontinuities at their respective phase boundaries. The pyrite-type phase has the lowest anisotropy with AP = 4% and AS = 12% at 120 GPa, consistent with its high-symmetry cubic structure and nearly isotropic elastic-wave propagation.

items.title: Topological Transitions of Evanescent Waves
items.summary: We study the band structure of evanescent waves, that is, the decaying or growing solutions that live within the gaps of tight-binding Hamiltonians. Although the underlying Hamiltonian is Hermitian, these modes carry complex wavevectors and therefore exhibit a non-Hermitian dispersion. Using the transfer matrix formalism in one dimension, we show that, in addition to the standard exceptional points that appear at the band edges, a different type of exceptional point can arise inside the gap, protected by spinless time-reversal symmetry. Tuning model parameters drives a topological transition where such in-gap exceptional points are nucleated in pairs, mediated by a crossing between purely imaginary momentum branches. We show that this spectral structure is diagnosed by a $\mathbb{Z}_2$ index assigned to every energy inside the gap, with the in-gap exceptional points arising as its domain walls. A generic bound state in the system has a tail that is purely exponential when its energy lies between a band edge and the nearest exceptional point, but becomes oscillatory - with a wavevector differing from the band-edge momentum - when its energy lies between the pair of in-gap exceptional points. We illustrate these results using continuum and tight-binding models, as well as an anisotropic photonic crystal.

items.title: Ground-State Dressing and Delayed Feedback of a Chiral Giant Atom in Ultrastrong Waveguide QED
items.summary: We study a chiral giant atom ultrastrongly coupled to a one-dimensional waveguide at two spatially separated points. At a relative coupling phase π/2, the total spectral density is independent of the distance between the coupling points, whereas its directional components are not. Using a variational polaron transformation, we show that the renormalized transition frequency and the total ground-state dressing inherit this independence, while the virtual-photon cloud remains chiral. A sudden switch-off of the coupling releases this cloud as directional radiation. We also derive the spontaneous-emission dynamics in the polaron frame, showing that, after neglecting the local photonic potential, the memory kernel becomes distance independent at the same phase.

items.title: Agnostic and efficient detection of $\mathbb{Z}_2$ symmetry-protected topological phases in projected entangled-pair states
items.summary: Symmetry-protected topological (SPT) phases are the simplest example of quantum phases that cannot be detected by local order parameters. Their classification is by now well-established from multiple perspectives, a prominent one being via tensor network states. The practical question, however, is not mere classification, but detection: given the ground state of an interacting Hamiltonian and a symmetry group $G$ along with its representation, is there an efficient way to tell if the state is in a SPT phase with respect to $G$? While there exist such practical tests in one spatial dimension (1D), methods in 2D have so far been restricted to finite-size systems or require an explicit form of virtual symmetries of the tensor networks representing the ground state. Here, we develop an agnostic and efficient method to detect interacting $\mathbb{Z}_2$ 2D SPT phases, using an infinite projected entangled-pair (PEPS) representation of the ground state. The method is agnostic to the symmetry representation in the virtual space of the PEPS tensor and applicable independent of the bond dimension of the tensors. Moreover, it is efficient as it does not require finite-size scalings: it works directly in the thermodynamic limit. We numerically demonstrate the procedure by mapping out phase boundaries away from fixed-point wavefunctions. We extract the SPT label cocycle data explicitly from the PEPS tensor.

items.title: Single-shot ground-state preparation via strongly coupled baths
items.summary: Preparing ground and thermal states of quantum many-body systems is a central task in quantum simulation. Dissipative protocols have emerged as a promising solution for both near-term and fault-tolerant hardware, but most constructions rely on weak system-bath coupling, leading to slow cooling. Here, we construct cooling protocols at strong system-bath coupling, and demonstrate accurate state preparation within even a single cooling cycle. Our protocols combine dynamically ramped ancilla energy levels with time-dependent couplings to optimize the trade-off between cooling error and physical time. For a general class of free-fermion systems, we reduce the dynamics exactly to a two-level scattering problem: ground-state cooling becomes a control problem of maximizing resonant excitation transfer while suppressing non-adiabatic heating. We then construct a family of ``Möbius-Ingham'' protocols, which reach optimal error scaling for gapless spectra and almost-exponential suppression of the leading heating error for gapped spectra, as a function of the cycle period. In our free-fermion benchmarks, Möbius-Ingham cooling lies on the Pareto frontier between steady-state error and cooling time among the controls tested. We further demonstrate its effectiveness in interacting Ising and $t$-$V$ chains and the two-dimensional Fermi-Hubbard model. Finally, we extend our construction to Gibbs state preparation, showing how free-fermion thermal states can be prepared in a single cycle.

items.title: Threshold-Free Symmetry-Enriched Topological Quantum Memory
items.summary: We show that non-Abelian symmetry enrichment can protect a toric code memory against incoherent electric noise at any bond error probability $p\in[0,1]$. For a toric code on the honeycomb lattice coupled to $Sp(N)$ rotors, with electric anyons carrying the fundamental representation, we construct an efficient minimum-weight decoder whose logical error probability decays exponentially with system size for $N\ge40$, a conservative sufficient bound. The same decoder also rules out strong-to-weak spontaneous symmetry breaking in the fundamental channel of $Sp(N)$ under the corresponding local decoherence in two dimensions. The construction extends to other symmetries, including $SU(N)$.

items.title: Constraint Variance Identity and the Matter-Geometry Fluctuation Relation
items.summary: The quantum Hamiltonian constraint vanishes for physical states. For separable Hamiltonians in minisuperspace, its vanishing variance yields a fundamental identity. Under the Born-Oppenheimer approximation, we derive the Matter-Geometry Fluctuation Relation, dynamically linking spacetime clock fluctuations to matter fluctuations. This establishes a quantitative stability condition for the clock against total quantum noise. Finally, we obtain an uncertainty relation between matter energy and relational time. The stable existence of spacetime thus demands quantum fluctuations in matter.

items.title: Chern-Simons Interfaces and Minimal Models from Quantum Groups
items.summary: Coupling two-dimensional fundamental Dirac fermions to $SU(N)_k$ Chern-Simons theory produces non-chiral interfaces that in the infrared flow to a compact boson and a $W_N$ minimal model. We propose a description of these interfaces as continuum limits of $q$-deformed fermion chains. The $q$-deformation is achieved by coupling a chain of one-dimensional fundamental complex fermions to $SU(N)_k$ Chern-Simons theory, keeping the underlying topological gauge field continuous. The operator algebra is controlled by quantum groups, which provide an algebraic perspective on the usual categorical formulation of anyon chains. As an application, we derive a Lieb-Schultz-Mattis constraint involving baryon-number and lattice translation, obstructing a unique symmetric gapped ground state. At unit filling, we gap out the compact boson sector with a Mott term and obtain standard anyon chain Hamiltonians previously studied in the literature. This provides an anomaly argument for the existence of $N$ copies of minimal model sectors permuted by lattice translation in the infrared.

items.title: Stability and Relaxation of Electron-Phonon Systems at Strong Coupling
items.summary: We study the kinetic properties of Migdal-Eliashberg theory (MET) for electron-phonon interactions at strong coupling. Previously, the system was found to be dynamically unstable at large couplings within a Markovian quantum Boltzmann approximation. Using the quasiclassical Kadanoff-Baym equation, we show that this instability is absent when non-Markovian effects are taken into account. We also analyze the long-time relaxation dynamics at strong-couplin, and find a clear imprint of the non-Markovian nature of the dynamics: in an intermediate temperature range between the Debye frequency and the coupling strength, the relaxation rate becomes linear in temperature with Planckian slope, while the leading relaxation mode acquires a large imaginary component, producing strongly oscillatory decay. Our results imply that any instability which preempts superconductivity must arise from effects beyond MET, such as phonon softening or polaronic effects at finite electronic bandwidth. This shows that the characteristic phonon frequency is not a fundamental bound on $T_c$, and leaves open a route to higher $T_c$ in multi-orbital electron-phonon systems.

items.title: Conformal Bootstrap Unblocked
items.summary: We develop a novel conformal bootstrap formulated directly in terms of conformal symmetry, reflection positivity, and crossing symmetry, without explicitly relying on the operator product expansion or conformal blocks. By constructing Gram matrices from states created by pairs of local operators and imposing spectral constraints through conformal generators, we obtain a hierarchy of semidefinite programs that directly constrain correlation functions. We demonstrate the method in one to three dimensions, obtaining correlator and spectral bounds that capture generalized free field behavior and reproduce the characteristic Ising kinks in two and three dimensions. We further show that joint positivity of states at different insertion configurations naturally constrains correlators away from self-dual kinematics.

items.title: On Entanglement Dynamics in Holographic Theories
items.summary: Entanglement entropy (EE) is central to modern theoretical physics, yet its calculation in interacting theories with nontrivial time dependence remains challenging. In this thesis, we investigate the real-time dynamics of EE in strongly coupled quantum field theories (QFTs) using the Anti-de Sitter/Conformal Field Theory (AdS/CFT) correspondence. We first examine EE evolution in an exactly solvable two-dimensional conformal field theory (CFT) with an inhomogeneous sine-square deformation (SSD). We argue that the unconventional time evolution driven by the SSD Hamiltonian can be viewed as a change in spacetime foliation, producing new horizons in the dual three-dimensional bulk. Holographic EE calculations agree with CFT results in all comparable cases. We then study entanglement dynamics in generic chaotic quantum many-body systems. In the limit of late time and large regions, these dynamics are believed to admit an effective entanglement membrane description. In 2d CFTs, a degenerate membrane tension reproduces several entropy dynamics results, unlike the non-degenerate tension in higher dimensions. Using holography, we show that capturing reflected entropy in 2d CFT requires an additional degree of freedom in the membrane description. We further show that a conventional non-degenerate tension emerges when the CFT undergoes a relevant deformation, holographically dual to a planar Banados-Teitelboim-Zanelli (BTZ) black hole with scalar hair and an interior Kasner universe. We then develop a membrane effective theory for reflected entropy dynamics in higher dimensions. Finally, we apply the membrane theories for reflected entropy to study the time evolution of multipartite entanglement signals. We found that scrambling dynamics generate multipartite entanglement with rich structures.

items.title: Nonlocal magic of fermions is bounded by entanglement fluctuations and is logarithmic for free fermions
items.summary: Free-fermion states are classically simulable, yet, written as qubits, they typically carry extensive magic, the quantum resource that stabilizer circuits lack. Part of this magic is nonlocal: local unitaries acting separately on two parts of the system cannot remove it. If these local unitaries are restricted to Gaussian ones, the nonlocal magic grows linearly with the number $m$ of partially entangled fermion pairs. We show that this growth is an artifact of the Gaussian restriction: local Gaussian unitaries minimize the nonlocal stabilizer Rényi entropy for up to three pairs, but not from four pairs on. General local non-Gaussian unitaries that respect fermion parity take $m$ free-fermion pairs to fermionic Bell pairs with a fidelity that decays at most as $1/\sqrt m$ compared to exponential decay with Gaussian unitaries, so the nonlocal magic drops from linear to logarithmic in $m$. The reason is statistical --- Bell pairs have equal Schmidt weights, that is, a fully degenerate entanglement spectrum, and a state can stay far from them only if its Schmidt weights are spread over many orders of magnitude. This spread is measured by the capacity of entanglement $C_E$, the variance of the entanglement Hamiltonian, and the nonlocal magic of any fermionic state grows at most logarithmically with $C_E$. Free-fermion pairs add to $C_E$ independently, so $C_E$ grows only linearly in $m$, and this leads to the stabilizer fidelity decreasing at most as $1/\sqrt m$. Almost all the magic of free fermions, including Hartree--Fock and BCS mean-field states, is therefore local.

items.title: Multipartite Entanglement, TQFT Partition Functions and PL Bordism
items.summary: In a previous work we conjectured that the multi-invariants of the ground state of a gapped $(d-1)+1$-dimensional system, labeled by bipartite $(d+1)$-edge-colored graphs encoding closed oriented $d$-manifolds $M$, compute the partition functions $Z(M)$ of the low energy topological quantum field theory (TQFT), up to non-universal factors determined by the local structure of the triangulation. In this paper we determine which combinations of partition functions can be isolated from the non-universal factors. The answer is governed by oriented bordism. If $M$ is null-bordant, $Z(M)$ is obtained from an explicit, state-independent finite family of multi-invariants, up to a power of $Z(S^d)$ which is fixed to be $Z(S^d)^{χ(M)/2}$ for even $d$ and can be removed for odd $d$. Conversely, the obstruction is measured by a quotient of the group of "residues" of colored graphs which receives a surjective map from the oriented bordism group, with kernel precisely the torsion subgroup as far as smooth manifolds are concerned. In $d=4$ the obstruction is the signature: $Z(M)/Z(S^4)^{χ(M)/2}$ can be extracted if and only if $σ(M)=0$. This is due to the fact that the first Pontryagin class $p_1$ has a local expression and thus $e^{iθσ(M)}=e^{\frac{i}{3}θ\int_M p_1}$ cannot be separated from the non-universal factors. Torsion invariants, in contrast, are not obstructed: for the ground state of the $4+1$-dimensional invertible phase with partition function $(-1)^{\int w_2w_3}$ we compute the multi-invariants exactly, and two graphs with identical local data, encoding the Dold manifold and $\mathbb{CP}^2\times S^1$, give opposite signs.

items.title: Large-Tiny Spin-Stripe SDW Order in La$_3$Ni$_2$O$_7$ via $^{139}$La-NQR Spectroscopy: Reconsideration Based on the $Am2m$ Structure
items.summary: The lower-symmetry $Am2m$ structure was recently proposed as the intrinsic ambient-pressure phase of La$_3$Ni$_2$O$_7$ based on synchrotron x-ray diffraction, whereas earlier studies investigated its properties assuming the commonly accepted $Amam$ structure. Here, we reexamine the crystal structure in La$_3$Ni$_2$O$_7$ and the spin configuration of spin-density-wave (SDW) state via $^{139}$La nuclear quadrupole resonance (NQR). The observation of two distinct La(2) sites in the NQR spectra is naturally accounted for by the $Am2m$ structure without any special assumptions, whereas it cannot be reconciled within the $Amam$ framework. Within the $Am2m$ framework, we reanalyze the spin configuration of the SDW phase and identify it as a large-tiny spin-stripe structure, arising naturally from two inequivalent Ni sites with large and tiny magnetic moments. These results establish the itinerant nature of the SDW order at ambient pressure in La$_3$Ni$_2$O$_7$, providing a basis for understanding its relationship to the emergence of high-$T_c$ superconductivity under high pressure.

items.title: Charged Three-Dimensional Solitons in a Ferroelectric Nematic Liquid Crystal
items.summary: Experimental observations and computer simulation of formation and structural properties of so far experimentally never seen electrically charged propagating 3D solitons are reported. The propagating solitons appear spontaneously without an external field in a ferroelectric nematic (NF) liquid crystal under rapid cooling from the antiferroelectric (SmZA) phase. The observed solitons propagate either parallel or antiparallel to the ferroelectric polarization and annihilate when they collide with each other. They are attributed to either positively or negatively charged propagating local polarization splay formed to screen excess negative or positive mobile charge lumps in the NF phase. The presence of mobile charge is attributed to a spatially periodic charge distribution present in the antiferroelectric phase that temporarily remains after the temperature is quenched through the antiferroelectric- ferroelectric phase transition.

items.title: Tree tensor network states represent low-energy states faithfully
items.summary: Extending corresponding results for matrix product states [Verstraete and Cirac, PRB 73, 094423 (2006); Schuch et al. PRL 100, 030504 (2008)], it is shown how the approximation error of tree tensor network states (TTNS) can be bounded using Schmidt spectra or Rényi entanglement entropies of the target quantum state. Conversely, one obtains bounds on TTNS bond dimensions needed to achieve a specific approximation accuracy. The result implies that efficient TTNS approximations exist if $α<1$ Rényi entanglement entropies for single-branch cuts obey an area law, as in ground and low-energy states of certain gapped systems on tree graphs.

items.title: Odd Capillarity
items.summary: Capillarity governs interfacial relaxation and hydrodynamic motion in binary fluids through parity-even mechanical stresses. Here, we introduce \emph{odd capillarity}, a parity-breaking interfacial mechanical response, by incorporating a symmetric, nonvariational, parity-odd capillary stress into the Cahn--Hilliard--Navier--Stokes (CHNS) equations. This stress generates forces along interfaces, transverse to ordinary capillary forces, and performs mechanical work that is not balanced by changes in the composition free energy. Direct numerical simulations reveal that odd capillarity arrests domain coarsening while sustaining turbulent fluid motion without a conventional inertial energy cascade, as energy injection is predominantly balanced by viscous dissipation. In asymmetric mixtures, odd capillarity driven deformation and breakup interrupt droplet growth, producing dynamically arrested emulsions with composition hyperuniformity and suppressed large-scale vorticity fluctuations. These findings establish odd capillarity as a distinct interfacial mechanism for controlling phase separation and sustaining nonequilibrium fluid motion.

items.title: Issue Editorial Masthead
Issue Publication Information
Enhancing light–matter coupling for exploring chaos in the quantum Rabi model
authors: Yan-Song Hu, Yuan Qiu, Ye-Hong Chen, XinYu Zhao and Yan Xia
items.summary: Accessing chaos in the quantum Rabi model (QRM) usually requires operating far from resonance, combined with ultra- or deep-strong light–matter coupling. This makes direct experiments challenging, so we propose an indirect route based on an anti-squeezing transformation of the bosonic field. This transformation maps a weakly coupled, two-photon driven Jaynes–Cummings model to an effective deep-strong-coupling QRM in the squeezed-light frame. Increasing the squeezing raises both the effective coupling and the atom–field frequency ratio, giving access to the semiclassical QRM regime without intrinsic ultra-strong coupling or large bare detuning. We analyze the chaotic behavior of the effective model using both semiclassical and quantum methods. These complementary diagnostics reveal coexisting regular and chaotic behavior and spectral correlations that depend on energy and squeezing. Long-time quantum features agree qualitatively with the semiclassical classification, whereas short-time criteria are not reliable stand-alone chaos tests in this model. Combining tunable coupling enhancement with these complementary probes provides a practical way to explore QRM chaos. Comparing the probe results also clarifies the limits of each method.

items.title: Unitary realizations of synchronizing automata in quantum systems
authors: Jȩdrzej Stempin, Jan Wójcik, Gabriela Banaszak, Andrzej Grudka, Marcin Karczewski, Paweł Kurzyński and Antoni Wójcik
items.summary: We introduce a quantum analogue of a classical synchronizing automaton. In the classical case the state of a system evolves according to a set of rules forming an alphabet, and sequences of these rules, called words, govern its evolution. Certain special words, known as synchronizing words, drive the automaton into a predetermined state regardless of its initial configuration. Although such an apparently irreversible process seems incompatible with the unitarity of quantum mechanics, we present a resetting protocol based on quantum synchronizing words by incorporating auxiliary qubits whose states encode the rules of the automaton’s alphabet. These qubits interact with the quantum automaton, whose state is encoded in a qudit, via a global unitary operation. When the qubit register is initially prepared in a state corresponding to a synchronizing word, the automaton evolves into a predetermined pure state independent of its initial state, while the qubit register is transformed into a complex, often entangled, state that encodes information about the automaton’s original configuration. The resulting entanglement depends on both the rule set and the automaton’s initial state, and we show how specific entangled states can be generated within this framework.

items.title: Inelastic Dark Matter and High-Energy Recoil Signatures in LZ
authors: Zi-Tong Fan, Hong-Jian He, Yu-Chen Wang and Yue Zhao
items.summary: We study the inelastic dark matter (iDM) that consists of two-component dark matter (DM) particles (χ1, χ2) and serves as a minimal extension beyond the commonly used one-component DM models. A distinctive feature of such iDM scattering with the target nuclei is to favorably produce signals at high nuclear recoil energy region in both exothermic and endothermic processes. In particular, for the exothermic DM scenario, the signal does not rely on the tail of the Boltzmann velocity distribution. As a result, the required DM–nucleus scattering cross section is significantly reduced, which in turn helps to substantially relax the stringent constraints imposed by IceCube neutrino searches. Using the iDM–nucleus scattering, we naturally explain the newly reported event excess at high recoil energy with the LUX-ZEPLIN (LZ) experiment.

items.title: Chiral Floquet Selection of an Algebraic Rydberg Bound State in the Continuum
authors: X. Z. Zhang, X.-F. Zhang and W.-M. Liu
items.summary: Bound states in the continuum remain localized despite the presence of extended modes at the same energy. In driven systems with long-range couplings, the absence of radiation does not by itself determine how a bound state decays in space. We study this problem in a Hermitian Rydberg spin waveguide, where a drive whose phase winds around a four-site plaquette combines rotation with time translation to exclude propagating guide channels from one symmetry sector. The resulting eigenstate remains embedded in the continuum of other sectors and carries an inverse-cube waveguide amplitude, with coherent contributions from direct plaquette–guide coupling and long-range guide propagation. Microscopic pair calculations determine the coupling in the axial Rydberg geometry, while coherent Floquet mixing accounts for the dominant angular-mode weight. The bound state thus retains the spatial signature of the long-range coupling even when radiation is forbidden.

items.title: Exceptional-Point-Like Sensing near Hermitian Transmission Peak Degeneracies
authors: Jiangshan Tang, 江山 唐, Longqi Xiao, 隆奇 肖, Haodong Wu, 浩东 吴, Yuwei Jing, 雨薇 景, Han Zhang, 涵 张, Yaping Ruan, 亚平 阮, Wuming Liu, 伍明 刘, Yan-Qing Lu, 延青 陆, Keyu Xia and 可宇 夏
items.summary: Non-Hermitian sensing near exceptional points can exhibit a sublinear response to perturbations and thus promises sensitivity beyond conventional Hermitian sensors operating at diabolic points (DPs). Recent studies have further shown that the square-root readout can be attained near transmission peak degeneracy (TPD), where the splitting of spectral extrema, not the eigenvalues, is observed. However, in non-Hermitian platforms, the available sensitivity enhancement is fundamentally constrained by the divergent Petermann factor because of non-Hermitian eigenvector degeneracy and practically limited by the system complexity. Here, we experimentally demonstrate TPD-enhanced sensing of refractive-index change in a simple chiral Hermitian cavity. We show that the Hermitian transmission spectrum can also exhibit TPD-induced square-root splitting of spectral extrema while preserving eigenvector orthogonality. As a result, this Hermitian TPD-based sensor retains the response enhancement characteristic of non-Hermitian TPD sensing yet remains free from the Petermann-factor limit intrinsic to non-Hermitian systems, thereby enabling enhanced sensitivity. This work establishes a Hermitian route toward ultrasensitive sensing that surpasses the conventional DP sensor and provides a sensitivity advantage over non-Hermitian implementations when Petermann-factor-amplified noise is relevant.

items.title: Heesch Weyl fermions in chiral antiferromagnets
authors: Zi-Ting Sun, Xing-Yao Guo, Ruo-Peng Yu, Xue-Jian Gao, Kam Tuen Law
items.summary: Weyl nodes are points in momentum space where two electronic bands touch linearly, each node carrying a chirality that makes it robust against small perturbations. Sun et al. identify Heesch Weyl fermions, symmetry-enforced Weyl nodes pinned at high-symmetry momenta in chiral antiferromagnets without Kramers degeneracy. Symmetry analysis and first-principles calculations reveal candidate materials, higher-order nonlinear Hall responses, and controlled node motion under strain, establishing a magnetic route to high-symmetry Weyl physics.

items.summary: Quantum-geometric nonlinear Hall (QgNLH) states characterize the quantum systems that exhibit the nonlinear transverse voltage-current responses with quantum-geometric origins. To functionalize QgNLH states, electrical manipulation is essential but remains challenging. Uchimura et al. demonstrated the electric-current manipulation of the QgNLH state by exploiting the interplay between the QgNLH state and the current-induced spin dynamics in a chiral antiferromagnet. This work opens opportunities for harnessing quantum-geometric nonlinear phenomena in practical devices that are essentially operated by electric current.

items.title: Measuring spin-charge separation by an off-diagonal dissipative response
authors: Liang Tong, Shi Chen and Yu Chen
items.summary: Spin-charge separation in the 1D Hubbard model is a paradigmatic example of quantum fractionalization described by decoupled charge and spin sectors of a Tomonaga–Luttinger liquid. Despite the success in measuring velocity differences, it remains challenging to probe emergent excitations’ anomalous dimensions experimentally. We propose an off-diagonal dissipative response protocol, leveraging dissipative response theory, to directly detect spin-charge separation. By selectively dissipating spin- particles and measuring the spin- response, we uncover a universal temporal crossover: the response grows as at short times and crosses over to linear-in- growth at long times. Specifically, the intersection time between the short-time and long-time linear growth exhibits a linear dependence on , whose slope is proportional to with a prefactor that depends on the filling , with negligible residual dependence on over a broad parameter range. This prefactor cancels when comparing slopes at a fixed , allowing the relative variation of with interaction strength to be extracted directly without any absolute calibration. Concurrently, the coefficient of the short-time law encodes the sum of anomalous dimensions through its spatial power-law decay. This response signal vanishes in the noninteracting limit, where spin and charge are not separated. Our predictions, verified numerically via time-dependent density-matrix renormalization group with microscopic parameters linked to Luttinger parameters by Bethe-ansatz, establish off-diagonal dissipative response as a self-contained probe of quantum fractionalization in synthetic quantum matter.
